claims.text: A Mo interlayer between W and CuCrZr will reduce the effective thermal-expansion mismatch.
A Mo interlayer will enhance bonding between W and CuCrZr.
The Mo-containing joint will have improved structural integrity under nuclear-fusion-reactor operating conditions.
Direct joining of W and CuCrZr produces interfacial stresses.
The interfacial stresses in directly joined W/CuCrZr arise from differences in thermal-expansion coefficients and mechanical properties.
A thin, controlled Mo interlayer can be introduced between W and CuCrZr during fabrication.
The Mo interlayer acts as a buffer that provides a gradual transition in mechanical and thermal properties between W and CuCrZr.
Mo has a coefficient of thermal expansion intermediate between those relevant to W and CuCrZr.
Mo has high-temperature stability suitable for this interlayer application.
Placing Mo at the interface will mitigate thermally induced stresses.
Thermal stresses at a direct W/CuCrZr interface can cause microcracking or bond failure.
Compared with a direct W/CuCrZr joint, a W/Mo/CuCrZr joint will exhibit greater interfacial integrity.
Compared with a direct W/CuCrZr joint, a W/Mo/CuCrZr joint will exhibit less crack propagation.
A W/Mo/CuCrZr joint will be more durable under thermal cycling and neutron irradiation than a direct W/CuCrZr joint.
Direct W/CuCrZr bonding typically has increased interfacial failure due to thermal-expansion mismatch.
Diffusion-induced stresses contribute to interfacial failure in directly bonded W/CuCrZr.
The effectiveness of a Mo interlayer may depend on its thickness and the fabrication method.
The effectiveness of a Mo interlayer may depend on neutron-irradiation intensity.
Extreme operating conditions may produce diffusion or microstructural changes in the W/Mo/CuCrZr joint.
The quantitative mechanical and thermal improvements under prolonged irradiation and thermal cycling remain undetermined.
